stories.headline: Fantasy hockey: The struggling players to drop and those you should hold on to
stories.summary: There are some slow starters you should move on from, and other with which to be patient or even trade for.
stories.body:
Just like that, we're already approximately one-eighth of the way through the 2026-27 NHL regular season. While there's still plenty of racetrack ahead, it's no longer too early to assess how some players are contributing -- or not -- to your fantasy team's success. With the help of Evolving Hockey in providing Individual Expected Goals (ixG) and Goals Saved Above Expected (GSAx) metrics for skaters and goalies, here's a handful of players to consider jettisoning already, plus a few early underachievers worth hanging onto a little longer.

More: Rankings | Most added/dropped | Mock Draft Lobby

Draft guide | Cheat sheet | Weekly picks | Sign up

Look elsewhere

Alex Ovechkin, F, Washington Capitals (0.9 FPPG, 87.1% rostered, 1.94 ixG): On this stacked Capitals' roster, the greatest goal scorer of all time doesn't need to produce like he has in the past. Which is handy, since he won't -- 13 shots through nine games! -- from his position on Washington's third line. At 41 years old, Ovechkin is back for one last tour to win another Cup, not chase down personal milestones. He'll produce in moderate fashion on the power play, and not too much else otherwise. Drop him and pick up second-year Ryan Leonard instead.

Matthew Knies, F, Columbus Blue Jackets (1.2 FPPG, 70.9% rostered, 2.56 ixG): After an explosive debut in which he potted two goals and an assist on four shots, the former Maple Leaf has since delivered essentially zilch. He isn't shooting and the team itself is an unsuccessful mess. How long until coach Rick Bowness shuffles Knies off the top line and power play out of desperate necessity? Not ages, that's for sure. While there's a handful of valuable fantasy performers on the worst team in the East, the 24-year-old power forward isn't one of them. Not right now.

Dylan Cozens, F, Ottawa Senators (1.1 FPPG, 74.7 rostered, 3.52 ixG): When fellow Senators forward Nick Cousins has more goals than your fantasy performer in Ottawa, it's a bit concerning. Sure, the second-line center is going to get on the board sooner rather than later, but what are your expectations of Cozens? Twenty goals? Maybe 25? On Travis Green's well-balanced roster, that's the expected haul. If you're battling in a shallower league, there may be superior available options with higher ceilings.

Karel Vejmelka, G, Utah Mammoth (0.8 FPPG, 92.6% rostered, -1.87 GSAx): The Mammoth are rumored to be in the market for a goaltending upgrade for good reason. If Utah's offense didn't average a seventh-best 3.73 goals/game, there's no way their No. 1 netminder would boast a winning record. Harboring a .871 save percentage and 3.04 goals-against average, he simply hasn't been good enough. Take another netminding route before Vejmelka's negative integers start to affect your weekly record.

Brandon Bussi, G, Carolina Hurricanes (-0.7 FPPG, 73.8% rostered, -1.46 GSAx): Helping his squad to a Stanley Cup victory is all fine and good but it's a fresh new season. One in which the still relatively inexperienced goaltender has struggled. Pyotr Kochetkov has been better (6-0-0) and GM Eric Tulsky is also thought to be on the hunt for another goalie to improve his squad. At minimum, right now I'd flip Bussi for Kochetkov, if possible.

Sergei Murashov, G, Pittsburgh Penguins (-1.4 FPPG, 55.2% rostered, -2.04 GSAx): Zero wins, along with a .883 save percentage and 3.50 goals-against average isn't the best start. Especially when your tandem mate is seeing more action and pocketing victories, including a shutout of the Panthers on Thursday. While the rookie netminder continues to develop, there are better goaltending options out there right now.

See also:

Jakub Dobes, G, Montreal Canadiens (-2.7 FPPG, 57.9% rostered, -3.9 GSAx)

Give it a minute

Sidney Crosby, F, Pittsburgh Penguins (1.3 FPPG, 96.8% rostered, 4.16 ixG): It almost feels like it should be against the law to suggest one of the greatest players of all time may no longer be suited for all fantasy leagues. But Crosby isn't shooting (much) or scoring. The Penguins collectively potted eight goals in their past two games and their captain didn't figure in on a single one of them. He also logged a season-low 16:39 in Thursday's win over Florida. I'm not ready to panic yet, but if Pittsburgh's superstar doesn't pull out of his funk by the second week of November, it will be time to take another direction.

Pavel Dorofeyev, F, New York Rangers (1.3 FPPG, 85.8% rostered, 6.1 ixG): The player some of us call Scorofeyev is going to be just fine. It's a new team, a new system, and a new coach. A little more time to adjust isn't too big an ask. The fact Evolving Hockey pegs the former Golden Knight at the top of their Rangers ixG table is also rather reassuring. Skating in the top six and on the No. 1 power play, Dorofeyev will start racking up goals soon enough.

Wyatt Johnston, F, Dallas Stars (1.6 FPPG, 95.6% available, 4.26 ixG): Getting that first one against Winnipeg on Thursday is going to help a whole heckuva lot. Skating more than 20 minutes/game on a top line and power play, and shooting a-plenty, the 23-year-old will start peppering his daily scoresheet with pleasing consistency. In fact, Johnston makes for an attractive trade target in leagues where his current manager might be feeling prematurely frustrated.

Brayden Point, F, Tampa Bay Lightning (1.1 FPPG, 82.8% rostered, 3.14 ixG): After last year's mediocre campaign, this season was supposed to be different; more like his successful seasons of old. Well, not so far. While the limited number of shots is one concern, falling off the top line, which includes Nikita Kucherov, is another. Still, Point remains on the club's No. 1 power play and the Lightning have competed in only nine contests. I'm giving the gifted center another couple of weeks before making any harsh decisions.

Timo Meier, F, New Jersey Devils (1.3 FPPG, 80.6% rostered, 4.73 ixG): It may be time to accept that the New Jersey version of Meier doesn't equate the model we enjoyed in San Jose. Still, the winger is shooting up a storm with the fifth-most shots in the league (43), and has little -- one goal -- to show for his efforts. No chance that 2.3% shooting percentage doesn't plump up in short order. Wait for Meier's inevitable productive eruption, then consider moving on before his next cooling off period.

Bowen Byram, D, Chicago Blackhawks (1.1 FPPG, 71.6% rostered, 0.33 ixG): While it's frustrating to wait out Byram's healthy return, I still want to see what he can accomplish when consistently sharing the ice with Connor Bedard. In their one overlapping game together, the defenseman rifled four shots on net and earned a power-play assist. Listed as day-to-day, his return shouldn't be too far off.

stories.headline: Brewers add pitcher Brandon Woodruff to World Series roster
stories.summary: Brandon Woodruff, who hasn't pitched in a game since July 4 due to a shoulder injury, took the place of Chad Patrick on the Brewers' World Series roster.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- Brandon Woodruff, who hasn't pitched in a game in 3½ months to a shoulder injury, was added to the Milwaukee Brewers' World Series roster in advance of Game 1 at American Family Field on Friday.

"I care about one thing, and that's winning," Woodruff said Thursday, before he knew the outcome of the Brewers' roster choices. "I know it's not an easy decision. Everything had to work out perfectly just to even have a shot at getting to this point."

Woodruff replaced righty Chad Patrick from the NLCS roster, leaving the Brewers once again with 13 pitchers and 13 position players heading into their matchup with the Tampa Bay Rays.

Woodruff, 33, is the longest-tenured member of the National League champions. He hasn't pitched in a game since July 4, when he exited an outing against the Arizona Diamondbacks with what was later diagnosed as an inflamed right shoulder -- the latest in a series of injuries that have plagued the righty in recent years.

Soon after, Woodruff told reporters he would undergo his second surgery in four years -- one that almost certainly would end his 2026 season. However, before undergoing the procedure, imaging showed enough healing to the point that Woodruff was cleared to start a throwing program.

That began a two-month rehabilitation process that culminated in Friday's announcement.

"Getting to the point where I'm at now was all I could ask for," Woodruff said. "It went as good as it could have gone. I've probably made their decision a little bit harder, which is a good problem for them. I'm lucky."

Woodruff's fastball velocity, which had dipped to 87 miles per hour on July 4, was reportedly at 92-93 mph during a simulated game earlier this week.

"This is a guy that's one of the most successful, dominant big-game pitchers I've ever been around," Brewers general manager Matt Arnold said.

While Woodruff's stuff appeared to be game ready, the decision to add him to the roster was not clear cut because of MLB rules around adding and subtracting players during a postseason series. Players that suffer new injuries can be replaced, so if Woodruff were to suffer a recurrence of his shoulder injury, the Brewers might have to play a player short.

"There are also some rule constraints that we're having to work through," Arnold said.

The ultimate decision to add Woodruff will add a boost to a Brewers clubhouse that hardly needs one after a franchise-record 103 wins in the regular season and a 7-1 start to their postseason.

He first joined the Brewers in 2017, one year before team captain Christian Yelich was acquired by the club. Injuries have always been an issue, but he's a two-time All-Star and finished fifth in 2021 NL Cy Young balloting.

Before his injury in July, he posted a 2.98 ERA over nine starts. More than the production though, Woodruff has become a veteran touchstone for the talented Brewers pitching staff, they youngest in baseball this season.

"Big Woo is an awesome human being," Brewers Game 1 starter Jacob Misiorowski said. "He's in there every day working."

The Rays will stick with 12 pitchers and 14 hitters, as they did during the American League Championship Series. The only change was the decision to replace righty reliever Brody Hopkins with lefty Garrett Cleavinger.

stories.headline: Transfer rumors, news: Barcelona to end up signing Sullivan?

stories.body:
Barcelona are among several major European clubs tracking Philadelphia Union midfielder Cavan Sullivan, while Como attacking midfielder Nico Paz is being watched by Chelsea and Manchester United. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

Real Madrid hold an €80 million clause to re-sign him, which becomes valid in early July, but Como are eager to keep the 22-year-old Argentina international after his two goals and an assist in their 4-1 Champions League victory over Manchester United.

With less than a year on his contract and talks over a new deal not progressing, the 32-year-old's high wage demands restrict his options in Europe, whereas Al Hilal remain attentive.

- Liverpool have held contact with representatives of Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha, reports Sky Germany. However, no formal offer is being prepared for the 26-year-old, with the Reds placing AS Monaco's Lamine Camara and Bournemouth's Alex Scott higher on their priority list.

stories.headline: UFC 333 preview and picks for featherweight, men's bantamweight titles
stories.summary: Check out the matchups and expert predictions for both championship fights at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi.
stories.body:
How does a fighter know when to stop when they're fighting well?

It's a question that, unfortunately, rarely gets answered in MMA. For every athlete who retires from the sport on their own terms, there are at least two athletes being retired by the sport. It is rare for a fighter to go out on a win, and infinitely rare for a fighter to go out on top.

UFC featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski (28-4) is starting to look that question in the face. Volkanovski will look to defend his title at UFC 333 on Saturday against 32-year-old Movsar Evloev (20-0) in Abu Dhabi, UAE. Volkanovski, 38, already is defying the rules of Father Time. In April 2025, he became the first fighter older than 35 to win a UFC championship belt in a weight class under 170 pounds. He defended that title in January against 31-year-old Diego Lopes.

In the past, Volkanovski has been dismissive, even comedic, of his age, starring in self-deprecating "Old Man Volk" skits on the internet. Ahead of UFC 333, however, he's been discussing age far more seriously, saying that any fight moving forward could be his last.

"There's a reason this is not often done," Volkanovski told ESPN. "I will bring up [my age], because I think it adds to the story. A lot of people are thinking about it. The young, undefeated guy -- facing the old, 38-year-old."

Evloev, of Russia, is one of the most proven title challengers in featherweight division history, with a perfect 10-0 record inside the Octagon, but he hasn't finished a single UFC opponent. He is a slight underdog against Volkanovski, according to DraftKings -- a credit to how good Volkanovski has looked, as well as lingering doubts on Evloev's ceiling.

Volkanovski, a two-time champion who suffered back-to-back knockout losses to Islam Makhachev and Ilia Topuria before regaining his title in 2025, told ESPN he believes he will actually look better than ever on Saturday, due to Evloev's style. The undefeated challenger is known primarily as a position-focused grappler, who might struggle to match Volkanovski's striking and scrambling ability.

"His style is a perfect matchup for me, I truly believe that," Volkanovski said. "I'm not delusional, saying I'm the best I've ever been at age 38. I'm not in my prime. But stylistically, I think you guys will be saying, 'I swear this is the best Volk we've ever seen.'"

Even if that is the case, odds say Volkanovski is tempting fate with every performance from this point forward. Male UFC fighters 38 and older have won 37% of their bouts all time, according to ESPN Research. Volkanovski has acknowledged as much and even proposed a "sendoff" title fight against 37-year-old lightweight champion Justin Gaethje next, after which they would both retire.

Volkanovski has stated he's taking it one fight at a time, but he is talking about retirement now, which shows he understands the decision is in front of him.

"One hundred percent, if I notice I'm slowing down or I'm taking more damage, [I'll retire]," Volkanovski said. "I said that before my last fight, too. A lot of people look at me saying that and say, 'Look how he's talking, his head isn't in it.' I'm just real and I'm honest. I said it before my last fight, and what happened? I went out there and made it look easy."

More storylines to watch

Dvalishvili looks to prove the last fight was an outlier
Merab Dvalishvili attempted to make history at the end of 2025, when he fought Petr Yan in his fourth men's bantamweight title defense of the calendar year. The feat has never been accomplished -- or even attempted -- and it proved to be too much as Dvalishvili lost a five-round decision. He later revealed he went into the bout with a significant knee injury and had a terrible camp. Dvalishvili (21-5) will try to recapture his title against Yan (20-5) in the UFC 333 co-main event.

Although he's admitted to tough circumstances around their last meeting, Dvalishvili has also said he doesn't regret pursuing UFC history and won't use those circumstances as an excuse, crediting Yan for the victory.

But the fighters' shared history has obviously raised the stakes for this Saturday. Dvalishvili and Yan have met twice, with Dvalishvili dominating their first meeting in March 2023. If Yan wins the trilogy, against a much fresher version of Dvalishvili than he saw in December, it could push Dvalishvili toward the back of the line for another title shot.

Not the last chance, but kind of the last chance
Not to put unnecessary pressure onto Aaron Pico's shoulders, but the truth is that any type of loss to Losene Keita -- a promising talent who is only 1-1 in the UFC -- would have heavy, long-lasting implications.

Pico, 30, has won 10 of his past 12 fights, but this is still a crossroads. He's been viewed as championship material since before his professional MMA debut, but has endured violent, memorable setbacks at various points in his career, including a spinning back elbow knockout loss to Lerone Murphy in his UFC debut 14 months ago. There is still massive potential in Pico, and he had an impressive bounce-back win against Patricio Pitbull in April, but he's in a risky position this weekend. He faces a dangerous but relatively unknown opponent in Keita after his original opponent, Arnold Allen, was forced off the card. Saturday's outcome will go a long way in determining how matchmakers and fans view him moving forward.

Coaches' questions and predictions for the title fights

Can Evloev significantly control Volkanovski on the ground?
Evloev is good everywhere, but Volkanovski has such an ability to game plan and show up in the big moments. Evloev is super big and strong. He has good standup, great transitions and ground control. But Volkanovski was able to get up after being taken down by Islam Makhachev. Are we just gonna forget that? Islam is now a welterweight. Volkanovski is so intelligent and so good at finding ways to exploit guys. His fight IQ is as good as anyone I've ever watched. He showed it against Lopes in their rematch in January. If Evloev cannot control Volk on the ground for long periods of time, Volkanovski will win a decision. And with the modern emphasis on damage when it comes to scoring, judges don't want to see you unsuccessfully try to hold someone down. Volkanovski by decision. -- Sayif Saud, Fortis MMA

Will age catch up to Volkanovski?
The biggest X factor is that unknown: At what point does Volkanovski's age slow him down? He's fighting one of the purest wrestlers/grapplers in the UFC in Evloev. I could see Evloev trying to prove he can stand with Volkanovski at times and win over the UFC, but I don't think that would be his smartest decision. Personally, I believe that "Old Man Volk" still has it. He's proven time and again he's going to win those key wrestling scrambles, and I believe he'll end up catching Movsar. It will be a grinder of a fight, but Volkanovski's experience being in there with bigger, stronger guys like Islam will pay off. Volkanovski by TKO. -- John Wood, Syndicate MMA

Can Dvavishvili hurt Yan with his hands?
We know that Yan has the physicality to compete with Merab's wrestling. He didn't avoid the takedown in their last fight -- he actually got more takedowns than Merab. That's a fact. And Yan on the feet is so dangerous, you have to give his standup the edge. If he comes in in great shape and can counter-wrestle and have the same physicality he did in December, he can win. The biggest technical question is whether Merab can create enough offense to get inside and hurt Yan with his hands. If the wrestling gets shut down, can he create offense? If Merab can hurt Yan on the feet, that changes the whole fight and throws it in favor of Merab. I've got Yan winning by a slight edge. -- Saud

Who will control the resets?
Yan needs to control the range, punish Merab's entries and continually invest in the body. He needs to establish the center and force Merab to initiate his wrestling from a distance, and intersect those entries with straight punches, body shots and uppercuts. I'd like to see him keep that lead arm frame, to establish his underhooks right away with his wrestling defense. He doesn't need to eliminate the takedown attempt, but he does need to make Merab pay for every failed attempt. Merab, meanwhile, has to weaponize pace, create chaos and disrupt Yan's comfort. He has to chain together multiple takedown attempts, so that even failed attempts affect Yan's rhythm. Who will control the resets? Merab thrives when one attack becomes three or four; Yan thrives when he's able to reset and return to technical striking. I lean Yan by decision again. --Eric Nicksick, Xtreme Couture

stories.headline: Wayne Rooney: Bruno Fernandes, Man United players acting like 'babies'
stories.summary: Wayne Rooney has lambasted Manchester United's squad for acting like "babies" and urged Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez to look in the mirror.
stories.body:
Wayne Rooney has lambasted Manchester United's squad for acting like "babies" and urged Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez to look in the mirror.

Fernandes followed Martínez in producing an eye-catching post-match interview on the back of Wednesday's 4-1 defeat at Como in the Champions League.

The result increased the scrutiny on Michael Carrick, who then faced criticism from Fernandes for the game plan in Italy but Rooney has accused the current United captain and Martínez -- who pointed the finger at Jason Wilcox -- of being selfish.

Sources: Carrick to lead Man United against Bournemouth

During an appearance on "The United Stand" podcast, Rooney, who also called for the board to provide clarity regarding Carrick's future, said: "When Martínez came out, I said this is an absolute nightmare because it will rip the dressing room apart. That was the start.

"We've seen it now with Bruno and you're going to see it with more players. The reason why is because them players don't want to take responsibility.

"You can say whether Bruno was right or wrong in what he said, but you have to take responsibility on the pitch, you have to take responsibility as a group of players and there were times when me and Sir Alex Ferguson wouldn't talk, but I'd run through a brick wall for him on the pitch.

"These players, they're selfish. They care about themselves, they don't care about their team-mates, don't care about the manager, about the staff or the fans, they care about themselves.

"If they're not getting what's right for them. They're like babies and just throw their toys out of the pram and go and deflect the blame on to anyone else but themselves. They have to look at themselves.

- Ogden: Who's to blame for Man United mess: Carrick, the players ... Ratcliffe?

- Dawson: Man United were abysmal in Como, but only Carrick who will suffer

"Bruno, he's having probably the worst run of form he's had since he's been at the club and again, it's no coincidence he's putting pressure on someone else because he doesn't want to face it.

"If he looks at himself in the mirror, if Martínez looks at himself in the mirror, all the players... they'll find what is looking back at them is them and it's not good enough."

stories.headline: Way-too-early AFL tiers: There's a clear flag favourite; 'silly season' winners and losers
stories.summary: Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers.
stories.body:
The 2026 AFL season is done and dusted, but that hasn't stopped ESPN's senior writer Jake Michaels from turning his attention to next year. Who are the 2027 flag favourites? Who are the legitimate contenders? And who should already be booking September holidays? It's our way-too-early edition of AFL tiers!

All of our best footy content, now on Instagram. Follow @espnfooty here!

Your new premiership favourite

1. HAWTHORN

Who knows if the Hawks would have been premiers this year if not for Hugh McCluggage's heroics late in that dramatic preliminary final at the MCG. There's certainly a real argument they would have gone all the way. This side, which is expertly coached by Sam Mitchell, just added Zach Merrett and Ben King to its best 23, two more experienced players desperate for flag success. There won't be many games the Hawks don't start favourite in next year. Even if this club's 2027 season over/under was set at preliminary final weekend, I'd still be taking the over.

Should be great, but there are some questions

2. BRISBANE

3. FREMANTLE

4. SYDNEY

The Lions just completed a remarkable three-peat and it certainly wouldn't have been outrageous for them to hold top spot here. But losing Lachie Neale and Chris Fagan -- arguably the two most important pieces of the club's modern-day dynasty -- cannot be underestimated. How do they fill those seismic gaps? The Dockers were the dominant team of the home and away season and if we played out the last four minutes of the Grand Final 100 times they probably win 99 of them. Instead, Fremantle has to spend all offseason dwelling on the greatest missed opportunity in club history. How do they respond in 2027? As for the Swans, who are always somewhere around the mark, nobody can really be sure what to expect after the Pullman Hotel saga. So many fascinating questions.

Silly season winners

5. GEELONG

6. WESTERN BULLDOGS

7. CARLTON

8. COLLINGWOOD

Each of these teams will be counting down the days until the 2027 season after drastically improving their lists during the trade and free agency window. The Cats landed the dynamic Toby Greene, significantly upgraded their ruck department with the singing of Rowan Marshall, and bolstered their defensive stocks with Jordan Ridley. The Bulldogs scored the biggest prize of all in Zak Butters, but they were also able to pry away Jordon Butts from the Crows, a much needed acquisition to what's been a shaky defence. The Blues will go into next season with Joel Amartey, Lachie Whitfield, and almost certainly father-son talent Cody Walker, while the Magpies added dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale and 2024 Coleman Medal winner Jesse Hogan.

Silly season losers

9. MELBOURNE

10. ADELAIDE

While a bunch of teams we'd expect to be in the fifth-to-10th range clearly improved their best 23, the Demons and Crows did nothing of the sort. Adelaide literally brought in nobody and will have to deal with the loss of key defender Jordon Butts, who departed as a free agent for the Bulldogs. Melbourne did sign several names, but do we think any of Zane Duursma, Will McLachlan, and Bodie Ryan can be needle movers in 2027? But hey, these were two sides I was down on this year and both ultimately outperformed expectations. Perhaps they do have it all figured out...

It's now or never

11. GOLD COAST

12. NORTH MELBOURNE

13. ST KILDA

If not now, then when? The Suns rocketed to co-flag favouritism this time last year after signing Christian Petracca and Jamarra Ugle-Hagan. They ultimately won just nine games and finished 13th on the ladder. Disastrous. Damien Hardwick is under serious pressure to get more out of this list. Meanwhile, the Kangaroos haven't played finals in a decade, but there's some newfound optimism after the senior coaching appointment of highly regarded Jaymie Graham and the signing of Nick Blakey, the biggest name the club has attracted in a decade. The Saints also need to show something early in 2027 or Ross Lyon could be on his way out ... again! But the real worry is not doing enough to ensure star midfielder Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera signs on.

It's going to be another long year

14. PORT ADELAIDE

15. GWS

16. WEST COAST

17. RICHMOND

18. ESSENDON

Perhaps I'm being a tad harsh on Port, who were pretty competitive this year. But at the end of the day we're taking Zak Butters out of a side that won just seven games. The Giants lost four of their best players in Toby Greene, Jesse Hogan, Lachie Whitfield, and Kieren Briggs, and will be relying heavily on their younger talent next year. And then there's the Eagles, Tigers, and Bombers -- three teams that combined for just nine wins this year. We all expect these sides to be somewhere around the bottom of the ladder.

stories.headline: 'No regrets': why Kangaroos prop made switch from Tonga
stories.summary: Keaon Koloamatangi has revealed why he couldn't knock back the opportunity to represent Australia at the World Cup after previously doing the same with Tonga.
stories.body:
Keaon Koloamatangi has revealed why he couldn't knock back the opportunity to represent Australia at the World Cup after previously doing the same with Tonga.

In recent years, the international scene has mostly showcased players with multiple heritages moving across from tier-one sides such as New Zealand and Australia to play for nations such as Samoa and Tonga in particular.

Koloamatangi went the other way, switching from Tonga to Australia before last year's Ashes tour after previously representing the Mate Ma'a on 10 occasions, including the 2022 World Cup.

"I just want to experience everything. I was lucky enough to play for Tonga in the last World Cup in England," Koloamatangi said

"I think if Australia comes calling, it's not something you can turn your back on. It's probably the best team you can make, and it's something I want to look back on, knowing I always dreamt of doing it as a kid."

Koloamatangi, who will join St George Illawarra next season from South Sydney, has a deep appreciation for both nations and does not regard his choice this time as valuing one side of his heritage over the other.

The 28-year-old will play prop against Fiji at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday night as a proud Kangaroo.

"I played for Tonga, I've play Origin, and I wanted to play for all the nations that I am eligible for," he said.

"It's something I'm really proud of because I'm just as Australian as I am Tongan. I was born Australian and my dad's Tongan. For me, I just wanted to experience a World Cup in the Australian colours, and I've got a lot of great mates here too."

Koloamatangi admits it was "a tough decision" but the classy response of Tonga coach Kristian Woolf reassured him.

"I spoke to Woolfy and he was very grateful for the conversation I had with him. He was respectful and accepted my decision. I have no regrets," Koloamatangi said.

"I loved my time with Tonga, with the atmosphere they get and the crowds they get.

"They're such a small country, and seeing them on the big stage now I've been being blessed to be a part of it."

There is a chance Tonga and Australia could meet in the World Cup semi-final or final.

Tonga's 30-12 win over England in the opening round has them on track to reach the final-four.

"I watched the game last week and was so proud of how they turned up for their nation," Koloamatangi said.

"Obviously, I want Australia to win, but if we weren't to win, I'll be cheering the Tongans all the way. I wish nothing but the best for them."
